# Rādha Saṁyutta (SN 23)

**ID:** SN 23
**Section:** Saṁyuttanikāya (sn)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-1
**Title (Pali):** Rādha Saṁyutta
**Title (English, SuttaCentral):** Linked Discourses with Rādha
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/sn23
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0303m.mul1.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Rādhasaṁyutta* (SN 23) is the twenty-third saṁyutta of the *Saṁyuttanikāya*, situated within the *Khandhavagga* and spanning pages 188–200 in volume III of the Pali Text Society edition [Bodhi 2000; Sujato 2012; Williams 2000]. The collection consists of four chapters (*vaggas*) comprising forty-six discourses, all addressed to the monk Rādha and focusing strictly on the analysis of the five aggregates (*khandha*) [Bodhi 2000; SuttaCentral]. While classified nominally under a specific person, the collection contains no personal or biographical narrative, functioning instead as a purely doctrinal collection and virtually serving as an appendix or offshoot spun out from the preceding *Khandhasaṁyutta* (SN 22) [Bodhi 2000; Sujato 2012; SuttaCentral]. According to the commentary (*Sāratthappakāsinī*), the Buddha favored Rādha when expounding subtle and profound topics [Bodhi 2000]. Prominent teachings in the collection include the exposition that the goal of dispassion is liberation (SN 23.1) [Anālayo 2019], the allegory in the *Sattasutta* (SN 23.2) of children dismantling their toy sandcastles as an image for dismantling and abandoning craving for the aggregates [Yinshun 2004], and the allegorical identification of Māra not as a personal mythological tempter, but with the five aggregates and all perishable phenomena (SN 23.1, SN 23.11–12) [Dayal 1932; SuttaCentral].

In both the Pali and Sarvāstivāda traditions, the Rādha and Diṭṭhi collections succeed the aggregate collection, functioning as *vyākaraṇa* (catechetical expositions) on the aggregates [Sujato 2012]. SuttaCentral identifies numerous full parallels in the Chinese *Saṁyuktāgama* (T 99), including SA 120 (for SN 23.1), SA 122 (SN 23.2), SA 112 (SN 23.4), SA 77 and SA 123 (SN 23.9–10), SA 124 (SN 23.11), SA 121 (SN 23.12), SA 127 (SN 23.19–22), SA 125 (SN 23.23), and SA 126 (SN 23.24) [SuttaCentral]. DharmaNexus corroborates these cross-language alignments with fascicles of T 99, while also detecting matches in Tibetan canonical texts such as the *Suvikrāntavikrami-paripṛcchā* [DharmaNexus]. Within the Pali canon, DharmaNexus records massive text reuse between SN 23 and the *Khandhasamyutta* (SN 22, sharing over 81,000 characters) and the *Saḷāyatanasaṁyutta* (SN 35, sharing over 73,000 characters), illustrating the systematic reuse of repetitive doctrinal formulas on the aggregates and faculties across the collection [DharmaNexus].
